Alhambra Planning Commission meeting will not be physically open to the public and the meeting will
take place via teleconference and video conference.

public access, members of the public can participate by using Zoom Webinar as follows:

For those wishing to speak on an agenda item, please email Principal Planner Paul Lam at
plam@cityofalhambra.org no later than 4:30 p.m. prior to the meeting with the item number you wish to
speak on and the phone number you will use when calling or the name you will use when logging into
the meeting. You should then call or log into the meeting at least 10 minutes prior to its start time. Staff

unless that time is adjusted by the President. If you do not have access to a computer please call 626-570-
5034 to request public comment.

As an alternative to speaking during the meeting, you can email your comments to the Planning Division

Any member of the public who needs accommodations or who needs their comments translated should
email or call the Community Development Department at plam@cityofalhambra.org or (626) 570-5034.

Section 2.24.060 of the Alhambra Municipal Code provides for the Planning Commission to establish and enforce

PROPOSAL
This is an application for a Planned Development Permit PD-21-10 and Conditional Use Permit
CUP-21-11 to construct a 78,600 square foot, seven (7) story 50-unit residential, and one (1)
commercial unit, mixed-use affordable housing apartment complex and a wireless facility on a site
of approximately 18,399 square feet located in the CBD and DRD (Central Business District &
Downtown Revitalization District) zone.

 LOCATION
The site is located on the east side of South 2nd Street, just south of West Main Street, between
Rick’s Burgers and the AT&T building. The site is currently a City-owned property developed
with a 42-space public parking lot. The site is also located in the Downtown Revitalization District
and is surrounded by commercial and mixed-use buildings with a variety of uses including
restaurants, retail stores, professional offices, and technical and professional schools. In addition
to the frontage along South 2nd Street, the subject property and the proposed building is also
accessible from an alley located to the north of the property.

BACKGROUND
The subject property (APN: 5344-026-915) is currently owned by the City of Alhambra and is
utilized as a public parking lot. On July 8, 2019, the City Council, in compliance with the surplus
land act laws then in effect, directed staff to issue a Request for Proposals (“RFP”) to allow non-
profit entities to submit proposals for an affordable housing project within Downtown Alhambra.
The RFP included language that required the replacement of some of the public parking spaces
that would be lost. The proposed project will provide a total of 24 public parking spaces that the
general public can utilize. On November 9, 2020, the City Council adopted Resolution R2M20-40
approving a Disposition and Development Agreement (DDA) to sell the land to the applicant and
to develop the proposed affordable housing project. The applicant will also be required to record
a Deed Restriction to mark the property as a low-income housing development, subject to a 55
year term (Condition of Approval PL12).

As part of the approved DDA, the City of Alhambra will utilize restricted Housing Asset Funds to
subsidize the 50 very low income units in this project. No General Funds will be expended to
pursue implementation of the proposed housing project, although the project will require a transfer
of the project site (a City asset) to the developer. City’s contribution will be made in the form of a
land sale and a construction loan. It is estimated that $1.2 M will be expended toward this project
in FY 2021-22.

  PD-21-10 & CUP-21-11
  Page 2 of 45
 ANALYSIS
The applicant is requesting approval for the construction of a seven (7) story 50-unit residential,
and one (1) commercial unit, mixed-use affordable housing complex with a 2-level above ground
parking garage. Residential uses are conditionally permitted in the CBD zone when in conjunction
to commercial use pursuant to AMC Section 23.28.030(X) [CPD Zone]. In addition, the applicant
is installing a new wireless facility at the western corners of the building along South Second
Street. The new wireless facility is a conditionally permitted use pursuant to AMC Section
23.28.030(W) [CPD Zone]. A Planned Development Permit is required for all new commercial
and residential developments pursuant to Section 23.62.020(A) and Section 23.62.020(B). The
applicant has also submitted the optional vesting SB330 Preliminary Review application. This
application provides vesting rights to the ordinances, policies, and standards adopted and in effect
upon submission and approval of the preliminary application. The preliminary application was
deemed complete on February 18, 2021.

The proposed development includes a total of 50 units, 30 of which are 1-bedroom units and 20 of
which are 2-bedroom units with three (3) layouts that prospective tenants will be able to choose
from. All units will share similar floor plans consisting of a living room, dining area, kitchen, and
one or two bedrooms. Plan 1-1 will consist of a one (1) bedroom one (1) bathroom of
approximately 648 square feet, Plan 2-1 will consist of a two (2) bedroom one (1) bathroom of
approximately 841 square feet, and Plan 2-1 Alternative will consist of a two (2) bedroom one (1)
bathroom of approximately 844 square feet. The residential units will be located on the floors three
(3) through seven (7).

Target Occupants
The proposed 50-unit mixed-use apartment complex will be developed for Supportive and Low-
income housing excluding one (1) unit for the Manager’s Unit. In accordance with Assembly Bill
(AB) 1763, Supportive Housing is considered affordable housing. The State of California Health
and Safety Code (HSC) 50675.14 defines “Supportive Housing” as “onsite or offsite services that
assist the supportive housing resident in retaining the housing, improving their health status, and
maximizing their ability to live and, when possible, work in the community.” A total of 24
supportive housing units will be constructed, with 15 units designated as a one (1) bedroom unit
and 9 units constructed as a two (2) bedroom unit. These 24-units will be income restricted for
those who meet the Area Median Income (AMI) of 30% (Very Low Income). In addition, 25
affordable units will be constructed, with 15 units designated as a one (1) bedroom unit and 10
units designated as a two (2) bedroom unit. These 25-units will be income restricted for those who
meet the AMI of 50% (Low Income).

Ground and Second Level
The ground level will be utilized mainly for commercial purposes, with 1,100 square foot
commercial space that the applicant has identified as a “cultural center” and a 550 square foot
lobby area that has direct access to the first and second floor parking garage. The applicant has not
yet provided any information on how the commercial space will be programmed as a cultural
center, however, the unit has the flexibility to be used as a commercial lease space, including retail
and office. Entry to the garage will be from the alleyway that runs between South 1st Street and

  PD-21-10 & CUP-21-11
  Page 3 of 45
 South 2nd Street, just south of West Main Street. The parking garage is located at the rear of the
complex, which is in conformance with General Plan Policy LU-2C. The garage will have a total
of 29 commercial parking spaces on the first floor and 23 residential parking spaces on the second
floor. The applicant is also proposing that 10% (or 3) of parking spaces will be prewired for EV
charging systems. A bicycle storage room will have a total of 50 bicycle parking locks, or one (1)
bicycle space per unit.

Third Floor
The third floor will consist mainly of communal facilities. There will be a 319 square foot leasing
office and 1,291 square feet of offices abutting a Community Room. The 972 square foot
Community Room will include a kitchenette, and an approximately 3,805 square foot common
open area. The common open spaces will be surrounded by an approximately 640 square foot
covered open space and a 3,165 square foot podium courtyard. The 1,291 square feet of office
space on the northwest corner of the building will be utilized by Social Workers and on-site
managers. These particular offices will not be operated by the leasing staff. Social Workers will
be using these offices to meet with residents on-site whom require their services. The rest of the
third floor will consist of only six (6) residential units.

Fourth to Seventh Floor
The fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh floors will have identical layouts consisting of 11 residential
units. Each floor will have a communal laundry facility room, a trash room, and two (2) residential
storage rooms.

Roof [Wireless Communication Facilities]
The proposed building will also have a wireless communication facility mounted at the western
corners of the Building behind the roof-top parapets along South Second Street. The cell tower
equipment area will be located next to the stairwell that leads to the roof-top staircase and the AC
systems. Wireless Communications Facilities are a conditionally permitted use within the CBD
zoning district. The Municipal Code requires all proposed wireless facilities to co-locate their
facilities with existing ones unless they are able to prove otherwise. There is an existing facility to
the south at the AT&T building on South Second Street. This facility has co-existing wireless
facilities along the building’s roof parapet on South First Street and South Second Street. However,
the proposed height of the affordable housing complex would exceed the height of the AT&T
Building along South Second Street. This would ultimately have a potential health and safety issue
with the existing wireless facilities mounted on the AT&T building along South Second Street, as
the frequency waves would radiate directly toward the proposed affordable apartment complex.
The applicant has worked with the owners of the wireless facilities mounted on the AT&T building
along South Second Street to have them relocated to the proposed affordable apartment building’s
roof to avoid this issue. The relocation of this particular wireless facility will also help the City
facilitate Policy SI-12A and Policy SI-12B of the Services and Infrastructure section of the General
Plan.

 Development Standards
The CBD zone does not require minimum setbacks, however there are minimum lot requirements.
Commercial properties in the CBD zone require a minimum lot size of 12,000 square feet and a
minimum lot frontage of 80 feet in width. The proposed mixed-use apartment complex is located
on a property with a lot size of 18,399 square feet and street frontage of approximately 87 feet in
width. The Alhambra Municipal Code prescribes maximum density, floor area ratio, height
standards, and minimum parking requirements, however, those standards and requirements are
superseded by AB 1763 being that this project is an affordable housing development located within
one-half (½) mile of a major transit stop. The proposed development meets the CBD development
and design standards as described in both the Alhambra Municipal Code and AB1763 and as
shown in the table below. The overall proposed project is required to provide a minimum of 20
parking spaces, and the applicant has provided a total of 52 spaces.

State Incentives
The proposed mixed-use complex consists of residential 49 affordable and/or supportive units and
one (1) manager unit. In accordance with AB1763, the project is defined as a 100 percent
affordable/supportive housing project. This project is subject to state incentives that are awarded
and governed by California. Under AB1763, the parking requirement shall be no more than a ratio
of 0.3 spaces per unit excluding the Manager’s Unit. The State also prohibits City staff, boards,
commissions, or any other governing body from requiring the applicant to provide parking beyond
the State calculated amount, including providing any Additional and Guest parking.

The Alhambra General Plan has a height limit of 5-stories for all development in the Central
Business District. However, AB1763 authorizes affordable and/or supportive housing projects to
surpass the height limit by no more than 3-stories or 33-feet per story in addition to the maximum
height. The proposed building meets the State’s height regulation, with the building not exceeding
7-stories.
  PD-21-10 & CUP-21-11
  Page 5 of 45
 The density and FAR are also governed by the State of California. The Alhambra Municipal Code
(AMC) would generally limit this project with regards to density and FAR, however, a
combination of AB1763 and Government Code 65915-65918 removes all density and FAR
restrictions the municipality may have. Therefore, the project has no applicable maximum density
or FAR.

Open space will be provided throughout the property in the form of common open space and
amenities. Although the Municipal Code requires 17,000 square feet of common open space at a
ratio of 300 square foot per dwelling units for one (1) bedrooms and 400 square foot per dwelling
units for two (2) or more bedrooms, the State’s density bonus law, Government Code 65915-
65918, provides the applicant the ability to request a smaller quantity through the use of Incentives
and Concessions. This project qualifies for up to four (4) incentives and concessions. Although the
applicant qualifies for up to four (4) incentives, the applicant is only proposing one (1) incentive
and concession, open space. A combination of AB1763 and Government Code 65915-65918
stipulates that municipalities shall approve the applicant’s requested incentive and concession
proposal unless there is an adverse effect on the public health or safety. The applicant has proposed
4,777 square feet of open space at a ratio of 95.5 square feet per dwelling unit. Open space will be
provided in the form of a covered outdoor area, a courtyard, and a community room. The
landscaping within the common open space area will contain various flowering plants, shrubs, and
accent trees. There will be no adverse effect on the public health or safety with this open space
design.

Design and Materials
As depicted in the rendering on the following page, a contemporary design style is used for the
project. The materials proposed include a brown brick veneer cladding which creates a pedestrian
scale to the street level, a high expanse of bronze storefront, and protruding white fiber cement
panels creates different steps in scaling the visuals to break the rectangular volume of the overall
building. By using different sized panels and by offsetting the openings from the rhythm of the
main building fenestration the white elements on the building effectively break the mass and
provide visual interest.

The second method is through color. Integrated with the aforementioned material changes, the use
of an overall brown colored building allows for the white elements on the building to define the
middle four (4) floors. Breaking the seven (7) levels into a 2-4-1 proportion provides a manageable
visual mass. The use of red accents in the recesses of the white frames offsets the brown color and
accentuates the openings of the white frames. The choice of brown window frames is consistent
with the aforementioned strategies so that the delineation within the fenestration does not distract
from the proportions of the building.

From the standpoint of architectural design, the location of this building type is appropriate as the
downtown area can support the proposed visual mass. The streets, visual setbacks and nearby
commercial and institutional buildings further strengthen the acceptability of the building height
and volume.

  PD-21-10 & CUP-21-11

 Traffic
In addition to AB1763, Senate Bill (“SB”) 743 is also applicable to the proposal. Aesthetic and
parking impacts of a mixed-use residential project on an infill site within a transit priority area
shall not be considered significant impacts on the environment in accordance with SB 743.
Pursuant to SB743, “Infill Site” means a lot located within an urban area that has been previously
developed, or on a vacant site where at least 75 percent of the perimeter of the site adjoins, or is
separated only by an improved public right-of-way from parcels that are developed with qualified
urban uses. Pursuant to SB743, “Transit priority area” means an area within one-half mile of a
major transit stop that is existing or planned, if the planned stop is scheduled to be completed
within the planning horizon included in a Transportation Improvement Program adopted pursuant
to Section 450.216 or 450.322 of Title 23 of the Code of Federal Regulations. These State
regulations are legislated as such to promote construction in an urbanized location and public
transit use. With the proposed development located in the downtown area, along with these
legislative immunities, this inimitable prospect will allow the City to meet General Plan Policy M-
2M-3A, R-5A, R-5B, and HS-7C, promoting compact development that encourages alternative
transit use.

The proposed project site is within a transit priority area and located in an urban infill site,
therefore, the project is exempt from providing a traffic analysis or conducting a VMT study.

HOUSING ACCOUNTABILITY ACT
Pursuant to California Government Code Section 65589.5, the Housing Accountability Act,
localities are prohibited from denying multifamily housing development projects that are
compliant with the locality’s Zoning Ordinance and General Plan at the time the application was
deemed complete, unless the locality can make findings that the proposed housing development
would be a threat to public health and safety (the prohibition appears to extend to single-family
projects, though the law is vague on that matter). The State also prohibits City staff, boards, or
commissions from conditionally approving a residential project by, reducing the height, density,
or any other objective zoning standards of a residential project or conditioning a project in such a
manner that renders the housing development project infeasible for development. “Reducing
density” is defined under State Code as:

  §5589.5(j)(5): “For the purpose of this section, “lower density” includes conditions
  that have the same effect or impact on the ability of the project to provide housing.

The proposed project meets or exceeds all applicable objective General Plan and zoning criteria of
a residential development in accordance with the Alhambra Municipal Code and meets all
incentives provided by the State of California.

HOUSING CRISIS ACT
Pursuant to California Senate Bill 330, the Housing Crisis Act, localities are prohibited from
conducting more than five (5) hearings held pursuant to its provisions, or any other law, ordinance,

  PD-21-10 & CUP-21-11
  Page 7 of 45
 or regulation requiring a public hearing, if a proposed housing development project complies with
the applicable, objective general plan and zoning standards in effect at the time an application is
deemed complete. If the city, county, or city and county continues a hearing subject to this section
to another date, the continued hearing shall count as one (1) of the five (5) hearings allowed under
this section. The bill requires the locality to consider and either approve or disapprove the housing
development project at any of the five (5) hearings consistent with the applicable timelines under
the Permit Streamlining Act. The inability to render a decision of the housing development project
at any of the five (5) hearings will result in an automatic approval of said project. The proposed
project has previously exhausted a total of two (2) hearings before the Design Review Board,
making tonight’s Planning Commission Hearing the third (3rd) hearing.

The Act is sharply in favor of the creation of housing and we are aware that housing advocates are
monitoring local agencies for compliance with the Act. In the interest of minimizing the City’s
exposure to litigation under that Act we provide the foregoing analysis.

ENVIRONMENTAL STATUS
This application is categorically exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act, Section
15332, In-Fill Development Projects, consisting of a project that is consistent with the applicable
general plan designation and zoning designation, occurs within City limits on a project site of no
more than five (5) acres, is located on a site that has no value as habitat for endangered, rare or
threatened species, would not result in any significant effects relating to traffic, noise, or air and
water quality, and is located on a site that can be adequately served by all required utilities and
public services.

PUBLIC NOTICE
On May 6, 2021, a Notice of Public Hearing was sent to 23 property owners and 34 tenants who
own or lease property within a 300-foot radius of the project site. A legal notice advertising the
public hearing was placed in the Pasadena Star News on May 4, 2021. A Notice of Public Hearing
was posted on the property on May 7, 2021. The Planning Division did not receive any comment
from the public at the time this report was finalized.

CONCLUSION
The proposed mixed-use project meets or exceeds all minimum objective requirements for a CBD
and DRD (Central Business District & Downtown Revitalization District) set forth in the
Alhambra Municipal Code, State Housing Density Bonus Laws, and development standards

SUBJECT:  Process Report Regarding Accessory Dwelling Unit’s (ADU’s)

PURPOSE
The purpose and intent of the information contained in this report is to provide the Planning
Commission with a general overview on the process of Accessory Dwelling Unit (“ADU”)
applications submitted to the City.

BACKGROUND
The item was brought back at the request of the Planning Commission on April 19, 2021, by a vote of
8-0-2. At the meeting Planning Commissioners requested a report outlining the ADU development
standards and the application process.

HISTORY OF ACCESSORY DWELLING UNITS
Prior to the state ADU legislation, the City had an ordinance in place since 2005 that regulated
“Second Units.” Local Second Unit ordinances were succeeded by ADU laws imposed by the State in
2017. The ADU laws allowed local agencies the ability to adopt a local ADU ordinance, including the
allowance of local standards and requirements, provided that the ordinance would not prevent the
construction of ADUs. The City adopted its own ordinance (Ordinance No. O2M17-4724) on
December 17, 2017, amending the City’s “Second Unit” ordinance consistent with State ADU laws.
Under the City’s ordinance, the City imposed some local standards and requirements including
minimum lot size requirements, maximum floor area ratio standards, restricting ADU size to no more
than 50% of the main building size, and owner occupancy requirements. As other cities adopted their
own ADU ordinances and incorporated their own local standards, the State saw these local
requirements as impediments to ADU development and as a result, the State revised the State ADU
laws in 2019. The amendments to the State ADU laws took effect on January 1, 2020 and took away a
local agency’s ability to impose standards such as minimum lot size, floor area ratios, maximum ADU
sizes, etc. Additionally, any local ADU ordinances that was not consistent with the new State laws,
including the City’s local ordinance, were automatically nullified on January 1, 2020.
 The City, once again, began updating the ADU ordinance in order for it to be consistent with new State
law. On March 16, 2020, Staff presented an amended ADU ordinance to the Planning Commission for
consideration and recommendation to City Council. The provisions of the amended ADU ordinance
essentially mirrored the State ADU laws. By unanimous vote, the Commission recommended that the
City Council approve the amended ordinance. At that moment, the COVID19 pandemic caused
cancellation of regular City public meetings and held special meetings, which were held on an as-
needed basis. As a result, it caused the ordinance to be placed on hold. Due to the circumstances that
followed, the city is now including the ADU ordinance with the citywide Zoning Update. In the
meantime, the city has been, and will continue to, implement the state ADU laws.

As of the January of 2020, the State amendment to the ADU laws permit the construction of ADUs
within all single-family and multi-family residential properties. However, JADUs are not permitted on
multifamily properties. The state also prohibited municipalities from imposing local regulations
regarding lot coverage, floor area ratio (FAR), open space requirements, number of bedrooms
permissible, and property size minimums on ADUs.

ADU TYPES
There are four (4) different types of ADUs:
  1.  New Detached;
  2.  New Attached;
  3.  Conversion of Existing Space; and
  4.  Junior ADU (JADU).
The four (4) types of ADUs, as outlined above, can differ in development standards and restrictions
based on whether the property is currently improved with single-family or multi-family residences.

SINGLE-FAMILY ADU DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS
ADUs are required by the state to meet specific development standards such as setbacks, height, and
parking. However, the state ADU laws also provide for certain exceptions or further restrictions to
these standards depending on the ADU type and/or location. The state provides these exceptions, not
the city.

Restrictions
The state ADU law requires a minimum height of 16-feet with a maximum height not to exceed the
municipality’s height restriction for that zone. An ADU can be two (2) stories with a restriction of 25-
feet in overall height. ADUs are also restricted to maximum overall size of 1,200 square feet. This
maximum square footage is only comprised of living space and does not include non-livable areas such
as balconies, porches, and garages. If an ADU is constructed within the existing footprint or attached
to the main dwelling, it cannot exceed ½ the overall square feet of the primary dwelling unit (i.e. an
attached ADU shall not exceed 600 square feet if the main dwelling is 1,200 square feet).

  SINGLE-FAMILY JADU DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS

  Page 2 of 4
   Junior Accessory Dwelling Units (JADUs) are a very small living units created within the
  existing main dwelling. The JADU must have a living/sleeping area, and a kitchen or
  kitchenette (i.e., stove or hotplate, refrigerator, and sink). A bathroom is not required, however
  if a bathroom is not provided, the JADU shall have direct access into the existing main
  dwelling unit.

  Limitations
  A JADU cannot exceed a total of 500 square feet and can only be placed within an existing
  dwelling or accessory structure. You can only construct a JADU if the property has proposed,
  or has an existing ADU. Any expansion of the existing main dwelling or accessory structure to
  accommodate the JADU shall be strictly for egress and ingress purposes and shall not exceed
  150 square feet. JADUs can only be constructed on a single-family residential property.

MULTI-FAMILY ADU DEVELOPMENT STANDARDS
A new element of the ADU law amendment of 2020 allows ADUs to now be constructed on multi-
family properties. Portions of existing multi-family dwelling structures that are not used as livable
space, including, but not limited to, storage rooms, boiler rooms, passageways, attics, basements, or
garages, can be converted into an ADU if each unit complies with state building standards for
dwellings.

Limitations
A detached ADU on a multi-family property must not exceed 16 feet in overall height, or one (1) story.
When an ADU is detached from the multi-family development, there shall be no more than two (2)
accessory dwelling units.

Multiple accessory dwelling units within the portions of existing multifamily dwelling structures that
are not used as livable space, is allowed at least one (1) accessory dwelling unit, up to 25 percent of the
existing multifamily dwelling units.

SETBACKS
ADUs are required to be setback four (4) feet from the side and rear property line. If the proposed
ADU is to take place entirely within an existing accessory structure or dwelling unit, then the ADU can
utilize the existing structure’s setback. Any new portion proposed beyond the existing structure’s
footprint shall meet the four (4) foot setback.

PARKING
Newly constructed ADUs are required to provide an extra parking space. This spaces can be covered
but is not required. In most cases, the existing driveway can be used as the extra parking space.
However, if the ADU is within ½ mile of a public transit line (including bus lines), then no parking is
required. Furthermore, any existing accessory structure or portion of an existing dwelling that is
converted into an ADU is exempt from providing extra parking. If an existing garage, carport, or

 covered parking space is demolished in conjunction with the construction of an ADU or converted to
an ADU, the City cannot require those off-street parking spaces be replaced.

ADU PROCESS
An ADU requires a Building Permit which applicants will obtain by submitting for Plan Check with
the Building Division. The Building Division will then route plans to each of the applicable
Departments/Divisions for review. Upon receiving departmental approvals, the applicant will then be
issued a Building Permit. Pursuant to state law, ADUs are subject to a state mandated 60-day review. If
an ADU application is deemed “incomplete” or has been provided corrections, the 60-day time clock is
placed on hold.

MORE INFORMATION
The Planning Division provides a clean and simple fact sheet located our website that offers the public
a chance to learn about the different types of ADUs, the regulations for ADUs, and the process of
which an ADU is subject to. The City’s ADU webpage has been available online since February of
2020 which outlines the standards and regulations and the how an ADU application is processed.
Information about ADU’s can be found on the City’s website at the following link:
https://www.cityofalhambra.org/resources/accessory-dwelling-unit.
